**PayPal joins European Payments Council as non-bank influence grows**

*PayPal has become a member of the European Payments Council, giving the US platform a direct voice in shaping SEPA payment rules and standards.*

PayPal announced on July 2 that it has joined the EPC, the body responsible for managing SEPA payment scheme rules and developing payment standards across Europe. The company will contribute to discussions on interoperability, instant payments and fraud prevention, according to Sean Byrne, who leads PayPal's European operations.

The EPC's membership has historically been dominated by banks and banking associations. PayPal's admission reflects the body's gradual opening to non-bank payment service providers, a shift that accelerated with PSD2 and will deepen further under PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation. With over 430 million active accounts globally and a regulated European banking entity, PayPal brings significant transaction volume and cross-border reach to the table.

For the EPC, the move signals recognition that scheme governance must reflect the diversity of institutions now operating on SEPA rails. For PayPal, it provides direct input into rule-making at a time when European payment sovereignty, instant payments mandates and account-to-account payment standards are all actively being reshaped.

*Sources: [PayPal Joins the European Payments Council](https://newsroom.paypal-corp.com/2026-07-02-PayPal-Joins-the-European-Payments-Council) — PayPal Newsroom | [PayPal Secures EPC Seat to Help Guide Future of European Payments](https://www.pymnts.com/legal/2026/paypal-secures-epc-seat-to-help-guide-future-of-european-payments/) — PYMNTS*

**Barclays, HSBC, Lloyds and NatWest adopt Swift retail payments framework**

*Four of the UK's largest banks will be among the first globally to go live with Swift's new framework for cross-border consumer payments, extending instant payment expectations to retail corridors.*

Barclays, HSBC, Lloyds and NatWest are adopting Swift's consumer payments framework, designed to bring the speed, transparency and predictability of domestic instant payments to cross-border retail transactions. The framework builds on Swift's existing correspondent banking network but adds standardised processing expectations tailored to consumer use cases such as remittances and person-to-person transfers.

The UK's early adoption is notable given the parallel domestic debate about next-generation retail payments infrastructure. HM Treasury launched a consultation on that subject last week, and the Payments Vision Delivery Committee published an updated policy paper on July 2 setting out roles and responsibilities in the future retail payments ecosystem. Swift's framework offers an international complement to those domestic efforts.

Cross-border retail payments have long lagged behind wholesale flows in speed and cost reduction. Swift's framework is an attempt to close that gap within existing infrastructure rather than building new rails, positioning it as a pragmatic alternative to CBDC-based or blockchain-native approaches to the same problem.

*Sources: [Major UK banks adopt Swift consumer payments framework](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48030/major-uk-banks-adopt-swift-consumer-payments-framework) — Finextra*

**Banks warn AMLA that instant payment speeds outpace real-time AML monitoring**

*Financial institutions have told the EU's Anti-Money Laundering Authority that the speed of instant payments is making real-time transaction monitoring operationally difficult, raising questions about how compliance will work under the new regime.*

Banks and crypto firms have warned AMLA that the near-instantaneous clearing of instant payments creates a fundamental tension with anti-money laundering requirements, according to AML Intelligence. Institutions report that existing monitoring systems struggle to screen transactions meaningfully before funds are irrevocably settled, particularly at the volumes instant payments now generate.

The warning arrives as the EU's instant payments regulation takes full effect and SEPA instant credit transfers become the default across the eurozone. The regulation requires banks to verify payees and process transfers within seconds, leaving a narrow window for sanctions screening, fraud detection and suspicious transaction reporting. AMLA, which became operational earlier this year, is still developing its supervisory approach to these challenges.

The tension is not new in principle — the UK has grappled with similar issues since Faster Payments launched in 2008 — but the scale is different. Europe's instant payments mandate applies across 36 countries simultaneously, and the compliance burden falls on institutions with widely varying levels of technical sophistication. How AMLA responds will shape whether instant payments compliance becomes a genuinely risk-based exercise or a box-ticking one.

*Sources: [Banks and crypto firms warn AMLA that transaction speed blocks real-time monitoring](https://www.amlintelligence.com/2026/07/banks-crypto-warn-amla-transaction-speed-blocks-real-time-monitoring/) — AML Intelligence*

**UK Payments Vision Delivery Committee sets out infrastructure roles**

*The PVDC has published an updated policy paper defining roles and responsibilities in the UK's future retail payments ecosystem, advancing the coordinated work between Treasury, the Bank of England and the PSR.*

The Payments Vision Delivery Committee published an updated policy paper on July 2 setting out how roles and responsibilities should be allocated in the next-generation UK retail payments infrastructure. The paper reflects coordinated work between HM Treasury, the Bank of England, the FCA and the PSR, and follows last week's Treasury consultation on the same subject.

The PVDC paper addresses the question of who does what in a future ecosystem that is expected to encompass the successor to Faster Payments, new account-to-account payment capabilities such as variable recurring payments, and integration with initiatives like UKPI. The committee is positioning itself as the coordination mechanism between regulators, Pay.UK and industry participants as this transition unfolds.

The timing is deliberate. With the Treasury consultation open, UKPI launching its first participants, and Pay.UK redesigning its liquidity model, the UK is managing several overlapping infrastructure transitions at once. The PVDC paper attempts to impose structure on what could otherwise become a fragmented process.

*Sources: [Payments Vision Delivery Committee update: Roles and Responsibilities in the future Retail Payments Ecosystem](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-payments-vision/payments-vision-delivery-committee-update-roles-and-responsibilities-in-the-future-retail-payments-ecosystem) — GOV.UK | [PVDC publishes updated policy paper](https://www.regulationtomorrow.com/2026/07/pvdc-publishes-updated-policy-paper-in-relation-to-roles-and-responsibilities-in-the-future-retail-payments-ecosystem/) — Regulation Tomorrow*

**Visa launches threat intelligence platform and runs agentic payments in Europe**

*Visa has introduced a cyber threat intelligence service for financial institutions and separately completed agentic commerce transactions with European banks, extending its push into AI-initiated payments.*

Visa announced two distinct initiatives on July 3. The first is a threat intelligence platform designed to help banks and payment processors detect and respond to cyber threats, drawing on Visa's visibility across its global network. The second is a series of agentic commerce transactions carried out with banks across Europe, building on the partnership with OpenAI announced last month.

The agentic payments activity places Visa alongside Mastercard, which completed Europe's first agentic payment with ING and Worldline in early June, and Crédit Agricole, which ran a production agentic payment in France shortly after. The competitive dynamic is sharpening: card networks, banks and open banking providers are all racing to define how AI agents will initiate and authorise payments.

The threat intelligence platform, meanwhile, reflects the broader industry recognition that payment fraud and cyber risk are converging. As instant payments and agentic commerce reduce human oversight of individual transactions, automated threat detection becomes a more critical layer of the payments stack.

*Sources: [Visa launches threat intelligence platform; carries out agentic transactions in Europe](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48032/visa-launches-threat-intelligence-platform-carries-out-agentic-transactions-in-europe) — Finextra*
